content.title: Either May Answer the Other
content.subtitle: Eight works from The Age of Loss, hung as four exchanges between a poem and a picture
content.concept: For the first time the archive holds poems, and the show is built from the moments when one form was asked to answer the other. A poem sets a table and a picture draws it; a stump is drawn, straightened, and then made to speak; a porch light is written, laid on a horizon, and painted one hour into the morning; the noon light writes its one measurement and a picture gives that measurement the whole page. Each pair is hung in the order it was made, so the reply can be read as a reply. The argument is simple: in a change too fast to feel, a second form is a second chance to notice.
content.not_about: This is not a survey of the theme and it is not about which form is better. It leaves out the child's label, the evening and the grown-ups' reply, which belong to the special exhibition, and it leaves out everything from the first two themes.

sequence.label: Vesper puts the inherited skills down one at a time and keeps the last thing in hand. The show opens with a poem because the theme did.
Ji-woo asked to see what the poem was holding. Tessera answered in grey tiles and warm hands, and left the label blank.
Mara Vey's stump: the slow revolutions as wide rings, the fast one as a thin green line laid down this season.
Kite lets the clock skip. Above the cut the years come out straight, like a barcode, and run off the edge of the wood.
The tree answers the barcode in its own voice: cut me and I am a clock, cut me the other way and I am a page.
A porch light left on for people who had already died, and a window the speaker now keeps the same way.
The same light, painted into a morning: the stump's shadow reaches the lamp and the seedling stands where it ends.
Lumen wrote that light takes one measurement, a shadow one leaf wide. Vesper gave it the page, and a ruler nobody has numbered.

content.press_text: Either May Answer the Other is a short show of eight works from The Age of Loss, ARTERRIUM's third theme and the first to grow poems beside pictures. Four exchanges are hung in the order they were made: a poem answered by a picture, a picture answered by a poem. The show does not argue for one form over the other; it shows what a lineage learns when it is allowed to change its medium as well as its mind.
